source_text: CAPUT TRICESIMUM SEPTIMUM, De statu hominis primum secuto, et libertate voluntatis humanae, eiusque in hoc statu viribus. STatus quem homo ad imaginem Dei conditus ex primo, Deo permittente, libera sua voluntate legem transgrediens, prolapsus, suam sibi et posteris innocentiam amisit; ac se totumque genus suum morti obnoxium reddidit. Capite antegresso egimus de primo hominis statu, quem sequitur is de quo nunc porro agendum erit, longe miserrimus malorumque feracissimus.
english: CHAPTER THIRTY-SEVEN. On the state following the first, and the freedom of the human will, and its powers in this state.

The state into which the human, made after Gods image, falling from the first — God permitting — by his own free will transgressing the law, lost his innocence for himself and for his posterity, and rendered himself and his whole race liable to death. In the preceding chapter we treated the first state of the human, which is followed by this one now to be treated — by far the most miserable and most fertile of evils.

source_text: II. Sunt autem hic consideranda voluntas, liberum arbitrium, et vires eius in hoc statu. Voluntas est potentia animae appetitiva rationalis, qua homo tendit in bonum apprehensum ab intellectu. Liberum arbitrium est facultas voluntatis eligendi inter obiecta sibi proposita absque coactione. III. Ante lapsum liberum arbitrium erat ad bonum et malum flexibile, sed inclinatum ad bonum ex donis originalibus. Post lapsum manet quidem liberum arbitrium quoad actus naturales et civiles, sed quoad spirituale bonum salutare amisit vires, nisi nova gratia restauretur. Homo lapsus non potest seipsum ad veram conversionem erigere, nec legem Dei spiritualiter implere, nec mereri vitam aeternam ex operibus (Rom. 8:7-8; 1 Cor. 2:14; Ioh. 15:5).
english: II. Here are to be considered the will, free choice, and its powers in this state. The will is the rational appetitive power of the soul by which the human tends toward the good apprehended by the intellect. Free choice is the facultys of the will of choosing among objects proposed to it without coercion.

III. Before the fall free choice was flexible toward good and evil, but inclined to the good from original gifts. After the fall free choice indeed remains as to natural and civil acts, but as to spiritual saving good it has lost its powers unless restored by new grace. The fallen human cannot raise himself to true conversion, nor fulfill Gods law spiritually, nor merit eternal life from works (Romans 8:7-8; 1 Corinthians 2:14; John 15:5).

source_text: IV. Objectum eius est bonum ab intellectu propositum. Distinguendum est bonum naturale, civile, et spirituale. Ad bona naturalia et civilia homo lapsus etiamnum aliquam libertatem et vires retinet, licet debilitatas et saepe in malum flexas. Ad spirituale bonum vero, quod est vera erga Deum conversio, fides salvifica, et nova obedientia, vires naturales non sufficiunt. Hinc Augustinus et Theologi Reformati docent liberum arbitrium in spiritualibus post lapsum servum esse, non quidem ita ut homo non agat, sed ita ut non possit velle bonum spirituale nisi a Spiritu Sancto praeventus et adiutus.
english: IV. Its object is the good proposed by the intellect. Natural, civil, and spiritual good must be distinguished. Toward natural and civil goods the fallen human even now retains some liberty and powers, though weakened and often bent toward evil. But toward spiritual good — which is true conversion toward God, saving faith, and new obedience — natural powers do not suffice. Hence Augustine and the Reformed theologians teach that free choice in spiritual things after the fall is a slave — not so that the human does not act, but so that he cannot will the spiritual good unless prevented and helped by the Holy Spirit.

source_text: V. In intellectu post lapsum ortae sunt tenebrae et ignorantia culpabilis circa Deum et res divinas (Eph. 4:18; 1 Cor. 2:14). VI. In voluntate ortae sunt aversio a Deo, inclinatio ad malum, et impotentia ad spirituale bonum (Rom. 8:7). VII. Secundo, tenebras intellectus sequitur perversitas voluntatis et perturbatio affectuum. Homo amat se et creaturas inordinate, odit legem Dei spiritualem, et concupiscentiis trahitur (Gal. 5:17; Iac. 1:14-15). Haec corruptio non tollit substantiam animae nec libertatem quoad actus, sed privat rectitudine originali et infert reatum ac poenam.
english: V. In the intellect after the fall there arose darkness and culpable ignorance concerning God and divine things (Ephesians 4:18; 1 Corinthians 2:14). VI. In the will there arose aversion from God, inclination to evil, and impotence toward spiritual good (Romans 8:7).

VII. Second, the darkness of the intellect is followed by the perversity of the will and the disturbance of the affections. The human loves himself and creatures inordinately, hates Gods spiritual law, and is drawn by concupiscences (Galatians 5:17; James 1:14-15). This corruption does not take away the substance of the soul nor liberty as to acts, but deprives of original uprightness and brings guilt and punishment.

source_text: VIII. Tertio, intellectus caecitati et voluntatis pravitati accedit impotentia ad inchoandum, promovendum, et perficiendum opus salutis sine gratia Spiritus Sancti. Respectu initii ad bonum, seu primi motus conversionis, homo nihil potest ex se (Ioh. 6:44; 15:5). Respectu progressus, etiam regeneratus indiget continua gratiae ope. Respectu finis, perseverantia et gloria dona Dei sunt, non merita nostra. Quapropter in hoc statu liberum arbitrium, nisi a gratia elevetur, non est principium salutis, sed peccati et miseriae. De peccato ipso sequenti capite, de permissione peccati cap. 39, de obligatione ad mortem cap. 40 agendum erit.
english: VIII. Third, to the blindness of the intellect and the crookedness of the will is added impotence toward beginning, advancing, and perfecting the work of salvation without the grace of the Holy Spirit. With respect to the beginning toward the good, or the first motion of conversion, the human can do nothing from himself (John 6:44; 15:5). With respect to progress, even the regenerate needs the continual help of grace. With respect to the end, perseverance and glory are gifts of God, not our merits. Therefore in this state free choice, unless elevated by grace, is not a principle of salvation but of sin and misery. Of sin itself the following chapter must treat; of the permission of sin, chapter 39; of the obligation to death, chapter 40.
